summary: Changes the IANA registration policy for Pool 3 of the Differentiated Services codepoint registry. Diffserv uses the DS field in IPv4 and IPv6 headers to carry one of 64 codepoint values, and this update to RFC 2474 changes how Pool 3 values may be assigned.

plainLanguage.summary: Packets carry a tiny label saying how important they are, and there are 64 possible labels. This changes the rule for who may hand out one group of those labels.

questions: what is the dscp codepoint space
why was pool 3 changed to standards action
what is the lower effort phb
subtitle: A small policy change that lets the IETF hand out Pool 3 Diffserv codepoints through Standards Action.

tldr.problem: Some per-hop behaviors need a DSCP value with particular bit properties, and the unassigned Pool 1 values do not have them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8436 changes the IANA registration policy for Pool 3 (codepoints of the form xxxx01) to Standards Action and removes its experimental and local use permission.
tldr.outcome: Pool 3 values can now be assigned through Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs, while Pool 2 stays available for experimental and local use.

today: RFC 8436 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2474. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the RFC Changes
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (Diffserv) uses the six most significant bits of the former IPv4 Type of Service octet, or the former IPv6 Traffic Class octet, to carry a DSCP. The DSCP value selects a per-hop behavior (PHB).

RFC 8436 is a short administrative update to RFC 2474. It changes the IANA registration policy for Pool 3 of the DSCP registry to Standards Action, and it removes the permission to use Pool 3 codepoints for experimental or local purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: This note changes the rule about who may hand out one group of packet labels. Before, anyone could try them out. Now they are kept for official uses.

sections.title: The Three Codepoint Pools
sections.content:
The six-bit field can convey 64 distinct codepoints. The codepoint space is divided into three pools for assignment and management.

  • Pool 1: 32 codepoints of the form xxxxx0, assigned by Standards Action as defined in RFC 8126.
  • Pool 2: 16 codepoints of the form xxxx11, reserved for Experimental or Local Use (EXP/LU).
  • Pool 3: 16 codepoints of the form xxxx01. RFC 2474 described them as initially available for experimental or local use, but to be used preferentially for standardized assignments if Pool 1 is ever exhausted.

At the time of writing, 22 of the 32 Pool 1 codepoints had been assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine 64 sticker designs split into three boxes. One box is for official stickers, one is for doodling, and the third was a spare box that could be used for either.

sections.title: Why Pool 1 Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Pool 1 is not yet exhausted, but some PHBs cannot use any of its unassigned values. The RFC's example is the Lower Effort (LE) PHB. It is designed to protect best-effort traffic from LE traffic in congestion: when resources become scarce, best-effort traffic has precedence over LE traffic.

In deployed networks, bleaching of the IP Precedence field (intentionally setting it to zero) continues to be used. That makes the first three bits of the old TOS byte zero. To avoid the LE codepoint being remapped, it needs a value whose first three bits are already zero.

If LE had been given an unused Pool 1 value with that property, bleaching would also remap other, higher assurance traffic onto the same DSCP. Diffserv-marked traffic could then get unintentional LE treatment for the rest of its path, a priority inversion. No unassigned Pool 1 codepoints have the needed properties, which motivates using a Pool 3 codepoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network gear wipes the first part of the label to zero. A label for low-priority traffic must survive that wiping, or important packets might get mistaken for unimportant ones. The unused official labels did not fit, so the spare box is needed.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 2474
sections.content:
The RFC updates Section 6 of RFC 2474. The old text said the Pool 3 codepoints were initially available for experimental or local use, but should be preferentially used for standardized assignments if Pool 1 is ever exhausted. The new text says they are utilized for standardized assignments, replacing the previous availability for experimental or local use.

It also deletes the footnote in RFC 2474 that said Pool 3 may be utilized for future Standards Action allocations as necessary.

The resulting policy is Standards Action for Pool 1, EXP/LU for Pool 2 and Standards Action for Pool 3.
sections.plainLanguage: The spare box used to be open for doodling. Now it is closed to doodling and only for official stickers. The doodle box stays open.

sections.title: What IANA Does
sections.content:
IANA changed the use of Pool 3 in the Differentiated Services Field Codepoints (DSCP) registry and manages it with Standards Action, which RFC 8126 defines as assignment only through Standards Track or Best Current Practice RFCs in the IETF Stream. Pool 2 is not modified.

IANA created a "DSCP Pool 3 Codepoints" subregistry, initially empty and formatted like the Pool 1 subregistry.

IANA is expected to normally assign from Pool 1 until it is exhausted, but it MAY assign from Pool 3 when the codepoint format has properties needed for a specific PHB. The document requesting such an assignment MUST explain the required characteristics in its IANA Considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: The keeper of the list starts with an empty page for the spare box. Anyone asking for one of its labels must explain why that exact label is needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that security considerations for the use of DSCP values are described in the RFCs that define their usage. It does not present new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: This note only changes who may give out labels, so it adds no new safety worries. Each label's own rulebook covers those.
